etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin topica, from Ancient Greek τοπικός (topikós, “pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical”), from τόπος (tópos, “a place”), of Pre-Greek origin.

definitions.definition: Subject; theme; a category or general area of interest.

quote.citation: 2013 August 3, “The machine of a new soul”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8847:
quote.text: The yawning gap in neuroscientists’ understanding of their topic is in the intermediate scale of the brain’s anatomy.

definitions.definition: (computing) A component similar to a message queue which supports multiple subscribers.
(music) A musical sign intended to suggest a particular style or genre.

quote.text: In Peircean terms, topics are interpretants: signifieds that become new signifiers in the endless semiotic chain of interpretations.

quote.citation: 1675, John Wilkins, Of the Principle and Duties of Natural Religion:
quote.text: contumacious persons, who are not to be fixed by any principles, whom no topics can work upon

definitions.definition: (obsolete, medicine) An external local application or remedy, such as a plaster, a blister, etc.

quote.citation: 1624, Democritus Junior [pseudonym; Robert Burton], The Anatomy of Melancholy: […], 2nd edition, Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  John Lichfield and James Short, for Henry Cripps, →OCLC:
quote.text: Amongst topics or outward medicines none are more precious than baths.
